tool.name: EnhancedHillshade
tool.summary: Computes a hillshade (shaded relief) raster from a single-band DEM, with correct results on geographic (latitude/longitude) rasters, optional hypsometric shading, vertical exaggeration, a configurable number of gray levels, and optional modeled cast shadows.
tool.usage:
The hillshade models the illumination of the terrain from a hypothetical light source at the azimuth and inclination you specify. Output values run from 0 (fully shaded) up to the number of hillshade levels (fully lit); 255 levels reproduces the familiar Esri hillshade range, while a small number of levels produces a posterized, cartographic effect.
Unlike the standard hillshade, this tool is accurate for DEMs in geographic coordinate systems: the horizontal and vertical dimensions of each cell are recomputed for every row of the raster from the spheroid, so slopes and shading are correct at any latitude without projecting the DEM first. Projected DEMs use faster constant-cell planar formulas. Elevation units are read from the DEM's vertical coordinate system when one is defined (geographic DEMs are assumed to be in meters); otherwise the tool asks you to choose meters or feet.
Hypsometric shading darkens the hillshade at lower elevations: at a strength of s percent, the brightness multiplier grades from (100 - s) percent at the minimum elevation up to 100 percent at the maximum, adding an impression of overall relief.
Cast shadows optionally dim any terrain that is hidden from the sun -- behind other topography -- to a chosen percentage of its unshadowed value (0 percent renders shadows black; the default 20 percent keeps some relief detail visible inside them). Shadows are computed with a single-pass sweep across the grid rather than per-cell ray tracing, so the option remains fast, but it requires reading the whole DEM into memory at once. On geographic DEMs the shadow sweep uses mean cell dimensions (the hillshade itself remains exact per row).
This tool is one part of the classic "Swiss style" of relief presentation (after Eduard Imhof and the Swiss cartographers, whose hand-drawn conventions Kurt Brassel first automated), which combines three strategies: illuminating the terrain from multiple directions, elevation-based tone adjustments that mimic atmospheric perspective, and softening of the final image. In this toolbox the MDOW Hillshade and Multi-Sun Hillshade tools provide the multi-directional illumination, the hypsometric-shading options and the Simple Hypsometric Shading tool provide the elevation-based tinting, and the Blurred Hillshade tool provides the softening.
By default the output matches the input grid exactly (same extent, cell size, and coordinate system). Honored environments: Processing Extent, Snap Raster, Cell Size, and Output Coordinate System, all applied as finishing steps to the computed hillshade -- the extent clips it (with the snap raster aligning the clip window), the cell size resamples it, and the output coordinate system reprojects it. Because the shading is always computed first from the full-resolution source DEM, cells at a clipped edge carry true hillshade values, and resampling or reprojecting smooths the finished shading rather than recomputing it on the new grid. The Mask environment is not honored, and pyramids are always built with bilinear resampling regardless of the Pyramid environment. The output carries statistics and a histogram so it renders correctly without a separate Calculate Statistics step. Reference: Horn, B. K. P. 1981. Hill shading and the reflectance map. Proceedings of the IEEE 69:14-47.
Symbolize the result with ArcGIS Pro's standard stretch renderers.

dialogReference.para: The elevation raster (DEM) to compute the hillshade from. It must be single band. Choose a raster from the map or browse to one on disk.
The output hillshade raster (integer, 0 to the number of hillshade levels; NoData where the DEM has NoData or at the outer edge). A suggested name is filled in from the input.

The DEM's elevation units, Meters or Feet. Filled in and locked automatically when the DEM defines a vertical coordinate system; geographic DEMs are assumed to be in meters. You are only asked to choose when the DEM does not say.
The compass direction of the light source, 0 to 360 degrees clockwise from north. The default 315 (northwest) is the cartographic convention.
The angle of the light source above the horizon, 0 (grazing) to 90 (directly overhead) degrees. The default is 45.

The number of gray levels in the output: values run from 0 (fully shaded) to this number (fully lit). Use 255 to match the standard Esri hillshade, or a small number for a posterized cartographic look. A larger number gives a higher-precision hillshade, although the added precision may not be visually apparent on a computer screen.
Darkens the hillshade at lower elevations to add an impression of overall relief. The amount is set by the Hypsometric strength parameter.

How strongly low elevations are darkened, 0 to 100 percent. At strength s, the brightness multiplier grades from (100 - s) percent at the minimum elevation up to 100 percent at the maximum. The default is 50.
Multiplies the elevations before shading, exaggerating (greater than 1) or flattening (less than 1) the relief. The default is 1 (no exaggeration).

Dims terrain that is hidden from the sun behind other topography to a percentage of its unshadowed value, set by the Shadow brightness parameter. Computed with a fast single-pass sweep rather than per-cell ray tracing; requires enough memory to hold the whole DEM at once.

The percentage of its unshadowed hillshade value that a shadowed cell keeps, 0 to 100. For example, at 20 percent a cell that would have been 100 is rescaled to 20. Use 0 for fully black shadows (the standard hillshade behavior) or larger values to keep relief detail visible inside the shadows. The default is 20.

scriptExample.title: Enhanced Hillshade example (stand-alone script)
scriptExample.para: Hillshade a geographic DEM with cast shadows and mild hypsometric shading.
scriptExample.code: import arcpy arcpy.ImportToolbox(r"C:\path\to\JennessEnterprisesTools.pyt") # your installed path is shown in this tool's run messages arcpy.jenness.EnhancedHillshade( in_raster=r"C:\Project\Elev.gdb\DEM_WGS84", out_raster=r"C:\Project\Elev.gdb\DEM_Hillshade", elev_units="Meters", azimuth=315, altitude=45, levels=255, use_hypso=True, hypso_strength=40, vert_exag=1, model_shadows=True)

dataIdInfo.idPurp: Hillshade with correct geodesic handling of geographic DEMs, hypsometric shading, and optional cast shadows.
dataIdInfo.idAbs: Computes a hillshade (shaded relief) raster from a single-band DEM. Cell dimensions on geographic DEMs are recomputed for every row from the spheroid, so shading is accurate at any latitude without projecting first; projected DEMs use planar formulas. Options: azimuth and inclination of the sun, number of gray levels (255 matches the Esri hillshade), hypsometric shading that darkens low elevations, vertical exaggeration, and modeled cast shadows (terrain hidden from the sun set to 0) computed with a fast single-pass sweep. The output matches the input grid (honoring the Processing Extent, Snap Raster, Cell Size, and Output Coordinate System environments as post-computation finishing steps) and carries statistics and a histogram.
